steps.label: Three small kernels also reach a seven-cell receptive field · 1/3

narration.label: p0-b1.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Begin at the single output position at the top and trace dependencies backward. It reads three neighboring positions in the previous layer; those collectively depend on five positions one layer earlier and seven positions in the input. This is a one-dimensional slice. In two dimensions, the corresponding receptive field is square. A stack’s final output is not restricted to just three positions of the original image.

It reads three neighboring positions in the previous layer; those collectively depend on five positions one layer earlier and seven positions in the input. This is a one-dimensional slice. In two dimensions, the corresponding receptive field is square. A stack’s final output is not restricted to just three positions of the original image.

steps.label: Three small kernels also reach a seven-cell receptive field · 2/3

narration.label: p0-b2.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The expansion depends on the stated conditions: three-by-three kernels, stride one, and no dilation at every layer. Each added layer increases receptive-field width by two, so L layers give two times L plus one. Three layers reach seven input positions. Matching that spatial extent does not make three nonlinear convolutional layers functionally identical to one seven-by-seven convolution.

steps.speakerNotes: Three small kernels also reach a seven-cell receptive field · 2/3 · Female: The expansion depends on the stated conditions: three-by-three kernels, stride one, and no dilation at every layer. steps.label: Three small kernels also reach a seven-cell receptive field · 3/3

narration.label: p0-b3.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The bottom formula makes a useful check. With four such layers, what receptive-field width do you obtain? Nine positions. This is the theoretical set of input positions that can influence an output, not a claim that all positions exert identical influence. Changing stride or dilation also changes the calculation, so this simple rule cannot be applied indiscriminately.

steps.label: Small-kernel stacking needs only 55.1% as many weights · 1/3

narration.label: p1-b1.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The upper comparison fixes every input and output width at sixty-four channels and excludes biases. A three-by-three convolution has nine times the channel count squared weights; three layers therefore have twenty-seven times the channel count squared, or one hundred ten thousand five hundred ninety-two weights. Fixing the intermediate channel widths is essential: wider hidden layers would change this count.

steps.label: Small-kernel stacking needs only 55.1% as many weights · 2/3

narration.label: p1-b2.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The single seven-by-seven kernel needs forty-nine times the channel count squared weights, or two hundred thousand seven hundred four. The small-kernel stack uses about 55.1 percent as many. But it also contains three ReLU operations rather than one. Equal receptive-field size does not make the functions equivalent, and this weight-count ratio should not be presented as an unconditional identical reduction in computation.

steps.label: Small-kernel stacking needs only 55.1% as many weights · 3/3

narration.label: p1-b3.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The takeaway combines efficiency with a structural difference. Can three convolutions with intervening ReLUs be replaced by one large linear convolution without changing the model in general? No. They can cover the same input extent, but the extra nonlinearities change the functions the network can express. This comparison saves ninety thousand one hundred twelve weights under the fixed-channel conditions shown.

steps.label: Convolution preserves size; pooling reduces it · 1/3

narration.label: p2-b1.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The left card assigns kernel width three, stride one, and padding one to convolution. Substituting these values into the size formula leaves the side length unchanged. Padding is doing that preservation work. Without it, each convolution loses two cells; a side of seven becomes one after three consecutive layers. Do not combine padded and unpadded dimensions as though they were one configuration.

steps.label: Convolution preserves size; pooling reduces it · 2/3

narration.label: p2-b2.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The right card uses pooling width two and stride two to halve an even side length. VGG separates feature extraction by convolution from spatial reduction by pooling. Five pooling operations follow the chain two hundred twenty-four, one hundred twelve, fifty-six, twenty-eight, fourteen, and seven. These values divide exactly; different input sizes still require checking rounding in the dimension formula.

steps.label: Convolution preserves size; pooling reduces it · 3/3

narration.label: p2-b3.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The takeaway is to keep a separate account for convolution and pooling. In the shown padded convolution, does a three-by-three kernel automatically reduce the side length? No. Padding one and stride one preserve it. Pooling is the operation that halves the even sizes in this example. Kernel size alone is insufficient to determine output dimensions.

steps.label: Five VGG-16 blocks contain thirteen convolutional layers · 1/3

narration.label: p3-b1.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The first three blocks show how depth, width, and spatial size change independently. Blocks one and two each contain two convolutions and use sixty-four then one hundred twenty-eight channels. Block three contains three convolutions and uses two hundred fifty-six channels. Pooling follows each block, so the feature maps become spatially smaller as their channel counts grow. Do not read the channel number as an image side length.

narration.label: p3-b2.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Blocks four and five each contain three convolutions and use five hundred twelve channels. Together the five blocks give thirteen convolutional layers, followed by three fully connected layers, hence VGG sixteen. The final convolutional representation is seven by seven by five hundred twelve. All VGG-sixteen convolutions are three-by-three; one-by-one kernels found in some other VGG variants should not be silently inserted into this version.

narration.label: p3-b3.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The bottom note distinguishes the specific model from its broader family. Do the five pooling operations count toward the sixteen in VGG sixteen? No: this convention counts thirteen convolutional and three fully connected layers. Most VGG variants omit LRN. Family-level statements should not erase the exact kernel and layer choices of the model under discussion.

steps.label: Wider channels make the same small kernel expensive · 1/3

narration.label: p4-b1.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The first two blocks show why fixed kernel size does not imply fixed parameter count. Every convolution uses a three-by-three kernel, but three input channels feeding sixty-four outputs require far fewer weights than sixty-four feeding sixty-four. Count nine times the input channels times the output channels. Keeping the spatial kernel fixed holds only one factor constant; the channel factors can still change dramatically.

narration.transcript: Female: The later rows contain five-hundred-twelve-to-five-hundred-twelve convolutions, each with two million three hundred fifty-nine thousand two hundred ninety-six weights. Parentheses indicate repeated layers and must be included in the sum. Adding all thirteen convolutional layers gives fourteen million seven hundred ten thousand four hundred sixty-four weights. These are weights only, without biases, so compare them with totals using the same convention.

steps.label: Wider channels make the same small kernel expensive · 3/3

narration.label: p4-b3.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The takeaway focuses on the two channel dimensions. If both input and output channels double while kernel width stays three, what happens to that layer’s weight count? It increases by a factor of four. This is why later wide layers can become expensive despite using the same small spatial kernel as early layers.

steps.label: The first fully connected layer is still VGG’s bottleneck · 1/3

narration.label: p5-b1.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: Compare all thirteen convolutions with the first fully connected layer. The convolutions together have about 14.71 million weights, whereas that first fully connected layer alone exceeds 102 million. The shared linear scale and zero baseline make the difference visible. Flattening the spatial map gives a separate classifier input for every position, which is the main reason this fully connected layer is so large.

steps.label: The first fully connected layer is still VGG’s bottleneck · 2/3

narration.label: p5-b2.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The other two fully connected layers add further storage. Together the fully connected layers contain 89.4 percent of all weights, and the first alone accounts for 74.3 percent. The total weight count is 138,344,128; adding 13,416 biases gives 138,357,544 parameters. Increasing convolutional depth does not automatically eliminate the fully connected memory bottleneck, and weights should not be confused with the bias-inclusive parameter total.

narration.label: p5-b3.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The bottom proportions provide a check on where compression might matter. Would removing a tiny number of early convolution weights address the largest storage component? Not by itself: the first fully connected layer dominates this configuration. This is a statement about parameter storage, not a complete comparison of runtime, activation memory, or predictive performance.

steps.label: Depth works together with the training recipe · 1/3

narration.label: p6-b1.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The first two cards combine the update rule with overfitting controls. Mini-batch stochastic gradient descent uses batch size two hundred fifty-six and momentum 0.9. More training data and L2 weight decay support generalization; the displayed decay coefficient is five times ten to the minus four. These settings act together, so the network’s behavior cannot be attributed to depth alone.

The source does not identify VGG’s initialization by name, so this slide does not invent one.

Also, the number of updates per epoch is a dataset-and-batch calculation; it is not the number of epochs used in training.

narration.transcript: Female: The original flattening keeps seven times seven times five hundred twelve values, for twenty-five thousand eighty-eight classifier inputs. Connecting every one to four thousand ninety-six outputs gives 102,760,448 weights in the first fully connected layer. Every spatial position supplies its own set of connections. That is the storage burden illustrated by the left card.

narration.label: p7-b2.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The right card averages the seven-by-seven positions separately within each channel, leaving five hundred twelve channel means. Multiplying five hundred twelve by four thousand ninety-six gives 2,097,152 weights, forty-nine times fewer. Only the first fully connected layer is being replaced in this comparison. This is an optional modification, not the original VGG-sixteen architecture, and averaging changes the spatial information available to the classifier.

steps.label: Averaging space reduces the first FC weights by a factor of 49 · 3/3

narration.label: p7-b3.mp3
narration.transcript: Female: The takeaway connects parameter saving to information retention. Why is the reduction factor forty-nine rather than five hundred twelve? Fewer connections do not mean the modified representation contains exactly the same positional information as the original flattened map.
